Semihydrogenation of Racemic Tetrasubstituted Allenes via a

ABSTRACT: The first earth-abundant transition metal Ni-
catalyzed highly regio- and enantioselective semihydrogenation of
racemic tetrasubstituted allenes via a kinetic resolution process as a
challenging task was well established. This protocol furnishes
expedient access to a diversity of structurally important
enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes and chiral allylic molecules
with high regio-, enantio-, and Z/E-selectivity. Remarkably, this
semihydrogenation proceeded with one carbon−carbon double
bond of allenes, which was regioselective complementary to the
Rh-catalyzed asymmetric version. Deuterium labeling experiments
and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out
to reveal the reasonable reaction mechanism and explain the
regio-/stereoselectivity.
■
INTRODUCTION
The chemistry of allenes with the intriguing structural
architecture of the orthogonal cumulative π-system has been
an area of considerable interest over the past few decades.
1−13
Allenes work as important building blocks with versatile
reactivity and have always been regarded as the hybrids of
alkenes and alkynes, which have been engaged in various
chemical reactions to access complicated skeletons. A number
of efficient transformations of mono- and disubstituted allenes
are well developed in modern organic synthesis; however, tri-
and tetrasubstituted allenes working as substrates have not
always been an easy endeavor and are less developed (Scheme
1a).
14,15
Among them, the carbometalation of allenes with
organometallic M−Nu intermediates always resulted in the
chemo- and regioselective generation of two disparate
carbometalated intermediates M-alkenyl INT (sp
2
-M bond
formation) or M-π-allyl INT (sp
3
-M bond formation; Scheme
1b).
16−21
These highly reactive intermediates went through a
variety of synthetic transformations and always required rare
and expensive noble-metal catalysts, including protonation,
annulation, β-hydride elimination, and reductive elimination,
providing structurally important organic molecules. Compara-
tively, the transformations of thermodynamically disfavored M-
alkenyl INT were challenging and reported scarcely. Among
these metal-catalyzed transformations, there are limited
examples involving the selective reduction of allenes, which
always result in intricate reaction systems, including full
hydrogenation products, four different stereoisomeric alkenes
from regio- and stereoselective semihydrogenation.
22−25
Therefore, it is an enormous challenge to realize the selective
reduction of allenes with high regio- and stereoselectivity. In
2017-, Dong and co-workers reported an elegant work that the
highly efficient Rh-catalyzed regio- and enantioselective
semireduction of 1,1-disubstituted allenes was first successfully
developed in the presence of a Hantzsch ester reductant
(Scheme 1c�left).
26
The more challenging tri- and tetrasub-
stituted allenes are difficult to achieve semireduction due to
their intrinsic difficulty. Recently, Zhang, Lv, and co-workers
developed Rh-catalyzed highly regio- and enantioselective
semihydrogenation of tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfones to afford
chiral allylic sulfones with excellent 1,2-regioselectivities and
high enantioselectivities (Scheme 1c�right).
27
Considering
the abundance in the earth, low price, and low toxicity of
nickel,
28−34
as well as the potential to give promising reactivity
and selectivity, until now, the semireduction of allenes,
especially challenging and fascinating tetrasubstituted allenes
substrates, promoted by cheap nickel catalysts has never been
explored. Therefore, it is highly desirable and important to
develop nickel-catalyzed asymmetric semihydrogenation of
challenging tetrasubstituted allenes in an excellent regio/
enantioselective manner, and there are several intractable

allenes promoted by an earth-abundant metal catalyst remains
unknown, (2) how to control the regio-, enantio-, and Z/E-
selectivity of semihydrogenation of allenes, and (3) the
cyclization or polymerization of allenes may result in low
reaction efficiency and poor selectivity.
On the other hand, considering the intriguing peculiarities of

addition to conjugated enynes and derivatives,

Despite these
noticeable recent advances, the direct asymmetric trans-
formations of racemic tetrasubstituted allenes to construct
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes are still not well-
established and are of great interest. Considering the
continuous interest in earth-abundant nickel catalytic sys-
tems
72−81
for the hydrogenation of allenes and the importance
of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes, we envision that Ni-
catalyzed asymmetric semihydrogenation of racemic challeng-
ing tetrasubstituted allenes via a kinetic resolution process
could offer the opportunity to access these two important
kinds of enantiomerically enriched molecules in the meantime
(Scheme 1d). Herein, we made notable efforts to develop an
inexpensive, earth-abundant first-row 3d transition metal nickel
catalytic system for the asymmetric semihydrogenation of
tetrasubstituted allenes and present our first results on Ni-
catalyzed highly regio- and enantioselective semihydrogenation
of racemic tetrasubstituted allenes via a kinetic resolution
process. It furnished an expedient approach to chiral allylic
molecules with high regio-, enantio-, and Z/E-selectivity and
axially enantioenriched tetrasubstituted allenes.
■

With the mild reaction conditions established, we then
sought to explore the substrate scope of this Ni-catalyzed
asymmetric semihydrogenation of tetrasubstituted allenes.
These reaction results are listed in Table 4. A series of
racemic aryl-substituted tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfones
bearing methyl and isopropyl groups were first exploited; a
wide range of substituted phenyl groups, which were electron-
neutral (3a), electron-donating (3b−c, 3f−h), and electron-
withdrawing (3d−e), could be well tolerated with excellent
reactivities, enantioselectivities, and KR performance (s-factor
up to 503). It was found that the length of the alkyl-substituted
group on the phenyl ring, such as t-butyl (3f), n-butyl (3g),
and n-hexyl (3h) groups, did not affect the reaction results in
this asymmetric transformation. To our delight, the 2-naphthyl
group with steric hindrance (3i) was also tractable in this
protocol, leading to the desired semihydrogenation product
(S,E)-4i and recovered (S)-3i with excellent results (s-factor is
266). When the isopropyl group of the substrate was replaced
by other sterically hindered alkyl substituents, for example, tert-
butyl (3j), cyclohexyl (3k), tetrahydro-2H-pyran-4-yl (3l), tert-
butyl piperidine-1-carboxylate-4-yl (3m), and 2,3-dihydro-1H-
indene-2-yl (3n) groups, they could still proceed smoothly to
give the corresponding products via an efficient KR process
with excellent results. We next explored the tetrasubstituted
allenyl sulfone substrates bearing other linear alkyl groups,
such as ethyl (3o), n-propyl (3p), and n-butyl (3q) groups,
which were compatible to give the recovered allenyl sulfones
with excellent ee values, albeit giving semihydrogenation
products (4o−4q) with diminished enantioselectivities. It is
possible that there is no discernible difference between these
linear alkyl groups and the methyl group, which led to the
remarkable difficulty of chiral catalysts in providing sufficient
enantiofacial differentiation during the reaction process.
Moreover, the tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfone substrate (3r)
bearing an ethyl group and a benzyl group worked well with
moderate results and a diminished s-factor of 8. We also
investigated the effect of the sulfonyl group on the reactivity
and selectivity. A range of tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfone
substrates bearing different electron-property groups on the
phenyl ring of the sulfonyl group (3s−3u) were applied in this
transformation. The expected semihydrogenation products
(4s−4u) and recovered (S)-3s−3u can be available with
moderate to excellent results (46−49% yields and 82−91% ee
for semireduction products 4s−4u; 42−44% yields and 94 →
99% ee for the recovered products 3s−3u, s-factor up to 93).

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were further
performed to investigate the detailed mechanism and the role
of the (S,S)-Ph-BPE ligand on regio- and stereoselectivity
(Figure 1).
83
Based on literature reports on phosphine-
coordinated nickel complexes, dimeric nickel complex
INT1A was set as the relative zero point for Gibbs free
energy (Figure 1a).
84
Initially, the loss of one acetate ligand by
intermediate INT1A results in the formation of dimeric nickel
cation intermediate INT2A with an endothermal energy of 3.7
kcal·mol
−1
. The decomposition of intermediate INT2A causes
the generation of cationic intermediate INT3A, which drives
the catalytic cycle of enantioselective semihydrogenation.
Meanwhile, the resulting neutral intermediate INT3B
dimerizes to regenerate INT1A. Subsequently, intermediate
INT3A undergoes acetate-assisted H
2
insertion through six-
membered nickel-acycle transition state TS4A with an
activation energy of 21.2 kcal·mol
−1
to deliver Ni−H species
INT4A (Figure 1a). The regioselectivity of the hydrogenation
can be illustrated by the frontier molecular orbital theory
(Figure 1b). For the structure of allenyl sulfone, its highest
occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is closely related to both
the electron-poor C2−C3 double bond and lone pair electrons
of the O atom, and its HOMO−1 orbital is associated with the
C1−C2 double bond. The lowest unoccupied molecular
orbital (LUMO) of the Ni−H species is contributed by the
Ni 3d orbital, which is 3.9 eV higher than the HOMO orbital
of allenyl sulfone and 4.4 eV higher than the HOMO−1 of
allenyl sulfone. The smaller LUMO−HOMO energy gap
illustrates that the Ni−H species preferentially interacts with
the HOMO orbital of allenyl sulfone. When the oxygen of the
two enantiomers 3a coordinates with the Ni(II) center of

CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have realized a challenging task for the first
earth-abundant transition metal Ni-catalyzed highly regio- and
stereoselective semihydrogenation of racemic challenging
tetrasubstituted allenes via a kinetic resolution process.
Remarkably, this work presented herein nicely regioselectively
complements the Rh-catalyzed asymmetric version, and one
carbon−carbon double bond of allenes was hydrogenated. It
represents a valuable advance in the construction of a wide
range of structurally important enantioenriched tetrasubsti-
tuted allenes and chiral allylic molecules with excellent results
(s-factors up to 780). Further studies of deuterium labeling
experiments and DFT calculations were conducted to explain
the regio-/stereoselectivity and elucidate the catalytic pathway.
